title: Permission-Aware Top-K Retrieval
statement:
A knowledge-base assistant answers questions from a team's documents. Before it calls the model, it retrieves the few documents most related to the question. Each document is shared with some groups, and a user must never see a document none of their groups can access.

Write def solution(docs, query, user_groups, k). docs is a list of dicts {"id": str, "text": str, "groups": [str, ...]}. user_groups is the list of groups the user is in.

Words. To get the words of a text: lowercase it, split it on spaces (several spaces in a row count as one), remove any . , ? ! characters from both ends of each word, and drop words that become empty. Other characters stay, so ready-made is one word. Apply this to both the query and each document; the query's words form a set, so a repeated query word counts once.

Rules.

  1. Access control comes first: a document is eligible only if it shares at least one group with user_groups. Ineligible documents are never scored.
  2. The score of an eligible document is the number of distinct query words that appear among its words.
  3. Drop documents with score 0.
  4. Sort by score, highest first; break ties by id in ascending string order.

Return the list of the first k ids (fewer if fewer documents remain).

examples.input: docs = [{"id": "d1", "text": "Leave policy. Staff get 14 days of annual leave.", "groups": ["hr", "all"]}, {"id": "d2", "text": "How to apply for leave in the HR portal?", "groups": ["all"]}, {"id": "d3", "text": "Server patching schedule for March.", "groups": ["eng"]}], query = "annual leave policy", user_groups = ["all"], k = 2
examples.why: d1 contains annual, leave and policy (the . after policy is stripped): score 3. d2 has only leave: score 1. d3 is in eng, which the user is not in.

examples.input: docs = [{"id": "a", "text": "Budget 2026 draft: salary bands and bonus pool", "groups": ["finance"]}, {"id": "b", "text": "Bonus pool FAQ for staff", "groups": ["all"]}, {"id": "c", "text": "Team lunch budget", "groups": ["all"]}], query = "bonus pool budget", user_groups = ["all"], k = 3
examples.why: a would match all 3 words, but the user is not in finance, so it is filtered out before ranking. b scores 2, c scores 1.

constraints: each text has at most 200 words; the query has at most 30 words

think.q: What decides whether a document appears, and in what order?
think.a: Two gates, then a sort. Gate 1: the user shares a group with the doc. Gate 2: the doc matches at least one query word. Order: more matched words first, then id.

think.q: Query leave policy, doc text Leave policy: 14 days?
think.a: Doc words: leave, policy:, 14, days. Only . , ? ! are stripped, so policy: keeps its colon and does not match. Score 1. Saying this out loud shows you read the spec.

think.q: What's the first thing you'd write?
think.a: Score every doc, sort everything, then filter by permission at the end. It returns the right ids only if you filter before cutting to k; filter after and the user gets fewer than k results, or worse, you leak the hidden doc into logs or prompts. Filter first.

"appears among its words", "shares at least one group" → set membership. Turn the query, each doc and the user's groups into sets; then a score is len(q & doc_words) and the permission check is allowed & set(groups).

1. Write words(text) once and reuse it.
  2. q = words(query), allowed = set(user_groups).
  3. For each doc: skip if no shared group; score; keep (-score, id) if score > 0.
  4. Sort the tuples and return the first k ids.

No docs. Empty query. A doc with no groups (visible to nobody). Ties on score. k bigger than the number of matches. Repeated query words. Punctuation and capitals. A high-scoring doc the user cannot see.

hints: Write a helper words(text) that returns a set: w.strip('.,?!') for each word of text.lower().split(), skipping empty strings.
Check permission with set intersection: if not set(user_groups) & set(doc['groups']): continue. Do it before scoring, never after.
Sort by two keys at once by storing (-score, id): Python compares tuples left to right, so higher scores come first and ties fall back to id order.
explain:
Retrieval for an assistant has two jobs: find relevant text and never show the wrong person the wrong text. The second job is not a ranking tweak; it is a filter that runs first.

  • Example 2: the user is in all. Doc a is only in finance, so the loop skips it before it computes any score.
  • Doc b: words {bonus, pool, faq, for, staff}. Query set {bonus, pool, budget}. Intersection size 2.
  • Doc c: {team, lunch, budget} ∩ query = {budget}, score 1.
  • Sorted tuples: (-2, 'b'), (-1, 'c') → ['b', 'c'].

Real systems replace word overlap with embeddings or BM25, but the shape stays: permission filter, score, sort, cut to k. If you filter after the cut, a user with narrow access gets fewer than k results; if you forget the filter, private text ends up in the prompt.
complexity: O(total words + m log m) time for m matching docs; O(words in one doc) extra space per doc

govtech.evidence: Practice shaped like the lab's public products (GovBrain); not a reported interview question.
extensions: Replace word overlap with BM25: rare words should count more than common ones. What extra data do you precompute per word (document frequency) and per doc (length)?
Build an inverted index word -> set of doc ids once, so a query touches only docs that contain at least one query word instead of all 5,000.
Add document chunks: each doc is split into paragraphs, you rank chunks, but return each doc id at most once (its best chunk). Where does deduplication go relative to the cut to k?

Groups change: a user is removed from finance. If you cached query results, how do you make sure the cache never serves a doc they lost access to? (Key the cache by the user's group set, or check permissions again on read.)
